Wroth
RAWTH
adjective
From Old English wrāþ, “angry, incensed, wrathful,” kin to wríþan, to writhe or twist—anger as the twisting or writhing of the mind. The predicate adjective of the noun wrath; it renders Hebrew chārāh (to burn, be kindled) and qātsaph (to be wroth).

Biblical Definition

Wroth is the old adjective of anger—to be wroth is to be incensed, kindled, hot with displeasure—and it is the writhing of the mind against what it will not bear. Its very first appearance is a warning: when the LORD had not respect to Cain’s offering, Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell (Gen 4:5), and the wrath of the rejected worshipper hardened swiftly into the murder of his brother. Jacob was wroth, and chode with Laban (Gen 31:36), the just indignation of a man long defrauded. Herod, mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth and slew the innocents of Bethlehem (Mat 2:16)—the fury of threatened power turned against the children. And in the Lord’s own parable the master, hearing of the unmerciful servant, was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors (Mat 18:34), a wrath that is wholly righteous and figures the just anger of God against the forgiven soul who will not forgive. So the word holds both a warning and a comfort. In man, wrath is mostly the flesh writhing at injury or affront, and Cain and Herod show whither it runs when unbridled—to blood. Yet there is a wrath that is holy: the settled displeasure of God against sin, slow, just, and terrible. Scripture bids us be ye angry, and sin not: the Christian is to eschew the wrath of Cain and to tremble before the wrath of the King, fleeing to the blood of Christ, which alone quenches the wrath we have deserved.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WROTH as very angry; much exasperated; incensed.

expand to see more

WROTH, a. — Very angry; much exasperated; incensed; hot with displeasure. Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell (Gen 4:5).

WROTH, a. — Moved to indignation, whether justly, as at a wrong endured, or unjustly, as in the fury of wounded pride.

WROTH, a. — Kindled in mind against a person or thing; stirred to the writhing displeasure that the word originally named.

WROTH, a. — Used of God, the settled and righteous displeasure of the Holy One against sin (Deu 1:34; Isa 57:17).

WROTH — A predicate adjective, closely allied to the noun WRATH, and now nearly obsolete except in the language of Scripture.

Key Scripture

Gen 4:5 — "But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect. And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell."

Gen 31:36 — "And Jacob was wroth, and chode with Laban: and Jacob answered and said to Laban, What is my trespass? what is my sin, that thou hast so hotly pursued after me?"

Mat 2:16 — "Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth, and sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently enquired of the wise men."

Mat 18:34 — "And his lord was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors, till he should pay all that was due unto him."

Modern Corruption

Not a redefined term but a word that exposes two errors of the age at once: the sentimentalism that denies God is ever wroth, and the license that excuses the wrath of Cain in man.

expand to see more

The modern temper commits two opposite faults, and wroth rebukes them both. On the one hand it will not have a God who is wroth—wrath is thought unworthy of love, and the settled displeasure of the Holy One against sin is edited out, leaving a deity too soft to save. Yet Scripture makes the Lord of the parable wroth at the unforgiving servant, and the whole gospel presupposes a real wrath from which men must be delivered. On the other hand the age excuses the wrath of Cain in man—the writhing rage of wounded pride that runs, unchecked, to violence of tongue and hand. Cain was very wroth and slew his brother; Herod was exceeding wroth and slew the children. The flesh baptizes its fury as righteous cause, and calls its writhing zeal. The word will let neither error stand: God’s wrath is real and just; man’s wrath is mostly the flesh, and deadly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold. First, confess the wrath of God as an article of the faith and a mercy of the gospel: his lord was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors—a warning to every forgiven soul who will not forgive, and a reason to flee to the blood of Christ, in whom alone the deserved wrath is quenched. Second, mortify the wrath of Cain: be ye angry, and sin not; let not the sun go down upon your wrath. The believer is to fear the one wrath and forsake the other—to tremble before the righteous displeasure of the King, and to slay in himself the hot, writhing anger that fells a brother and dims the countenance.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English wrāþ (angry), kin to wríþan (to writhe) — anger as the twisting of the mind; rendering Hebrew chārāh (to burn) and qātsaph (to be wroth).

expand to see more

Old English wrāþ — angry, incensed, wrathful; the predicate adjective allied to the noun wrāþþu, wrath.

Old English wríþan — to writhe, twist, bind; picturing anger as the writhing or twisting of the mind.

Hebrew chārāh (H2734) — to burn, be kindled, grow hot with anger (Gen 4:5, Cain very wroth; 31:36, Jacob wroth).

Hebrew qātsaph (H7107) — to be wroth, break out in anger (Gen 41:10; Lev 10:16; Deu 1:34).

English wrath, writhe — the surviving native kin, keeping the sense of burning displeasure and twisting distress.

Usage

"Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell—the first wrath in Scripture, and a warning of whither the flesh’s fury runs when a rejected worshipper will not master it."

"Herod was exceeding wroth and slew the innocents: the rage of threatened power turned against children, the wrath of Cain enthroned."

"His lord was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors—the righteous wrath of the King against the forgiven soul who will not forgive, a warning to flee to the blood of Christ."
